title: Jeremiah 38:14–28
context: King Zedekiah summons Jeremiah to a private meeting at the third entry of the LORD’s house and asks him to hide nothing. Jeremiah fears for his life and doubts the king will listen, so Zedekiah swears secretly to protect him. Jeremiah then sets the choice before the king in the LORD’s name: surrender to Babylon’s princes and live, with the city spared, or refuse, and the city will burn and he will be taken. Zedekiah admits his fear of the Judeans who had already defected; Jeremiah urges him to obey and describes what refusal will bring. The king asks Jeremiah to keep the conversation secret and tells him what to say to the princes, and Jeremiah stays in the court of the guard until Jerusalem falls. For the outcome—Zedekiah overtaken in the plains of Jericho, judged at Riblah, his sons killed, his eyes put out, and taken to Babylon in fetters—compare 39:5–7, 52:8–11, and 2 Kings 25:5–7; these accounts are named without harmonizing, and 52:11 adds that he was kept in prison until his death. On conditional words of what would happen, see the existing keyContrast at 1 Samuel 23:12.

verses.text: Then Zedekiah the king sent and took Jeremiah the prophet to himself into the third entry that is in the LORD’s house. Then the king said to Jeremiah, “I will ask you something. Hide nothing from me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah takes Jeremiah to the third entry of the LORD’s house and asks him to hide nothing. Arminian readers see a king who still wants the truth, even after letting the prophet be cast into the dungeon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the setting at the LORD’s house, fitting for seeking a word from God. Shared ground: both traditions read the request as genuine curiosity mixed with fear, which the conversation will reveal.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “If I declare it to you, will you not surely put me to death? If I give you counsel, you will not listen to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks whether the king will kill him if he speaks, and says the king will not listen anyway. Arminian readers see realism born of experience: the prophet knows how his words have been received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an honest assessment of the king’s heart, already shown by his past response. Both traditions read Jeremiah’s caution as reasonable, not faithless, and they note that the prophet still goes on to speak.

verses.text: So Zedekiah the king swore secretly to Jeremiah, saying, “As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death, neither will I give you into the hand of these men who seek your life.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah swears secretly by the LORD, who made their souls, that he will not kill Jeremiah or hand him to his enemies. Arminian readers note the king’s oath by the Creator, which binds him to protect the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the oath an acknowledgment of the LORD as the giver of life, even by a king who will not obey him. Shared ground: both traditions read the secrecy of the oath as revealing the king’s fear of his own officials.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “The LORD, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you will go out to the king of Babylon’s princes, then your soul will live, and this city will not be burned with fire. You will live, along with your house.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah declares the LORD’s word: if Zedekiah goes out to Babylon’s princes, he and his house will live and the city will not burn. Arminian readers see a genuine offer with real consequences hanging on the king’s choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the offer as sincere, and as God’s means of confronting the king with his duty. On conditional words like this, both traditions point to the existing keyContrast at 1 Samuel 23:12 rather than adding a new one here.

verses.text: But if you will not go out to the king of Babylon’s princes, then this city will be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they will burn it with fire, and you won’t escape out of their hand.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: If he refuses, the city will be given to the Chaldeans and burned, and he will not escape. Arminian readers note that the alternative is stated as plainly as the promise, leaving the king fully informed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the two paths as setting life and death before the king, compare Deuteronomy 30:19 by reference. Both traditions read the warning as real and serious, and they let the outcome in chapter 39 do its own work.

verses.text: Zedekiah the king said to Jeremiah, “I am afraid of the Jews who have defected to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah says he fears the Jews who have defected, that they might mock him if he is handed to them. Arminian readers see how fear of shame can keep someone from obeying a clear word from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear of people outweighing the fear of God in the king’s heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the confession as honest and sad, and they do not build a contrast over the king’s fear.

verses.text: But Jeremiah said, “They won’t deliver you. Obey, I beg you, the LORD’s voice, in that which I speak to you; so it will be well with you, and your soul will live.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah assures him they will not hand him over, and begs him to obey the LORD’s voice so his soul may live. Arminian readers see the prophet’s earnest pleading, showing God’s desire for the king’s good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an urgent call to obedience, with the promise of life attached. Both traditions read the plea as compassion from a prophet who, after all he had suffered, still sought the king’s welfare.

verses.text: But if you refuse to go out, this is the word that the LORD has shown me:
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says that if the king refuses, he will tell what the LORD has shown him. Arminian readers note that the warning follows the plea, giving the king every reason to choose life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet introducing a revealed vision of the consequences of disobedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a transition from appeal to warning, both grounded in what the LORD has shown.

verses.text: ‘Behold, all the women who are left in the king of Judah’s house will be brought out to the king of Babylon’s princes, and those women will say, “Your familiar friends have turned on you, and have prevailed over you. Your feet are sunk in the mire, they have turned away from you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah describes the women of the king’s house brought out to Babylon’s princes, saying his friends have turned on him and his feet are sunk in mire. Arminian readers note the echo of Jeremiah’s own experience in the mire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see poetic justice: the king who let the prophet sink in mire will find himself sunk and abandoned. Both traditions read the image soberly, as a lament the women will raise over the king’s betrayal by his own advisers.

verses.text: They will bring out all your wives and your children to the Chaldeans. You won’t escape out of their hand, but will be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon. You will cause this city to be burned with fire.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says the king’s wives and children will be brought out, he will be taken, and he will cause the city to burn. Arminian readers note the weight of the phrase you will cause, placing responsibility on the king’s refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s choice as the means through which God’s announced judgment comes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as sobering, and they name 39:6–7, 52:10–11, and 2 Kings 25:7 as later accounts without harmonizing them.

verses.text: Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, “Let no man know of these words, and you won’t die.
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to let no one know of their words, and he will not die. Arminian readers see a king more concerned with secrecy than with acting on what he has heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s fear of his officials again governing his response. Both traditions read the request as revealing the gap between hearing the word and obeying it, without turning the king’s fear into a doctrinal point.

verses.text: But if the princes hear that I have talked with you, and they come to you, and tell you, ‘Declare to us now what you have said to the king; don’t hide it from us, and we will not put you to death; also tell us what the king said to you;’
verses.arminianNotes: The king anticipates that the princes may come demanding to know what was said, promising not to kill Jeremiah. Arminian readers note that the king knows his own officials well enough to predict their tactics.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the court’s suspicion and intrigue laid bare, a setting hostile to truth. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as background to Jeremiah’s answer, showing the danger he faced from the princes.

verses.text: then you shall tell them, ‘I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathan’s house, to die there.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The king tells Jeremiah to say he begged not to be returned to Jonathan’s house to die. Arminian readers note that this request had in fact been made (37:20), so the answer is true as far as it goes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the earlier plea and see the reply as a partial account rather than a false one. Both traditions recognize that readers weigh the ethics of the answer differently, and they do not build a doctrinal contrast on it.

verses.text: Then all the princes came to Jeremiah, and asked him; and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they stopped speaking with him, for the matter was not perceived.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes question Jeremiah, and he answers as the king commanded, so they stop speaking with him. Arminian readers see the prophet protecting his life by withholding what he had no duty to tell them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records the outcome without comment, leaving readers to reflect on it. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as survival in a dangerous court, reported without praise or blame.

verses.text: So Jeremiah stayed in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah stays in the court of the guard until the day Jerusalem is taken. Arminian readers see the prophet preserved through the siege, his words proven true by events he lived to witness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithful keeping of his servant until the end of the siege. Both traditions read the closing line as a bridge to chapter 39, and they name 39:14 as the account of his release from the court of the guard.
